source.title: Evaluating Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts Antibody Language Models
source.authors: Sarah M. Burbach; Simone Spandau; Jonathan Hurtado; Bryan S. Briney

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure values are not legible in the supplied text, so only the results explicitly described in the text are recorded.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares held-out masked-language-modeling loss across antibody language models with different MoE routing architectures, and evaluates downstream tasks across model sizes. It does not reproduce a scaling-law sweep or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling laws as background but does not fit loss-versus-parameter, token, or compute laws, test extrapolation, or find compute-optimal allocations. Rows are limited to its own architecture-comparison loss results and its downstream classification comparisons. Other MoE routing and padding-token findings are not included unless they bear on the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study compares MoE routing strategies and MoE against dense models in antibody masked language models. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only in the Discussion, as background. It fits no loss-versus-parameters, tokens or compute curves, tests no extrapolation and runs no fixed-compute allocation sweep. Swapping routing schemes, or sparse for dense, is not the depth/width/shape variation at fixed parameter count that V4 names. The MoE models also differ in total versus active parameters, which the authors say confounds attribution. The two-size downstream comparison (Dense-200M vs Dense-710M vs BALM-MoE) is not a test of downstream predictability with scale or loss. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that token-choice routing, especially Top-2, outperforms expert-choice routing, which they attribute to expert specialization in CDRH3 residues. They find that masking pad tokens in routing improves loss. BALM-MoE beats dense models at both matched active and matched total parameters on masked-language-modelling loss, but trails Dense-710M downstream, likely because of its smaller embedding dimension. They invoke scaling laws only to predict that MoE benefits will grow as paired antibody data scale.
record.recipe_differences: This is an antibody-language-model architecture and routing comparison, not a scaling-law parameter/data/compute sweep or compute-optimal allocation experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss varies with routing strategy, expert capacity, and shared-expert configuration. The authors caution that capacity/shared-expert changes also alter total parameter count, complicating attribution. Downstream comparisons also vary in embedding dimension.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed 45M active parameters, the MoE routing strategy strongly changes antibody masked-language-modelling loss. Expert-choice models greatly underperform token-choice models and mostly underperform the 45M dense control.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In sparse MoE language models at matched active parameters, routing strategy changes loss substantially.

fits_no_version.finding: A Top-2 MoE with 200M active and 710M total parameters has lower masked-language-modelling loss than both a 200M and a 710M dense model, but worse downstream classification than the 710M dense model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE models can beat dense models matched on total parameters in pretraining loss, without matching gains on downstream tasks.

record.peer_reviewed: Published as a workshop paper at ICLR 2026; the text also identifies the bioRxiv version as not certified by peer review.
record.problems: The pilot models were trained for the same number of steps, which the authors say disadvantages larger models that converge more slowly. Capacity and shared-expert changes also change total parameter count, making their effects difficult to separate. Several comparisons are described qualitatively in text while exact plotted values are not legible in the supplied text. The study does not conduct scaling-law fits or extrapolation tests.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for every pilot capacity/shared-expert configuration because the supplied text does not provide legible per-configuration values; aggregate textual findings and the stated exception are recorded in R1-R3. Other router analyses and padding-token interventions do not bear directly on the claim versions catalogued here.

untested.parts: No power-law fits of loss against parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No depth/width/shape sweep at fixed parameter count. Only MoE routing and sparse-vs-dense comparisons are made.
Protein/antibody masked language models are studied, but no power-law form is fitted.
No predictive relationship between scale or loss and downstream performance. There are only two dense sizes plus one MoE model.
No analysis of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 and V6 links over-read the study. Comparing routers or MoE against dense is not V4's shape-at-fixed-parameter-count claim. The pilot configurations do not even hold total parameters fixed, and the authors also note that equal training steps disadvantage the larger models. No study-level labels are given. The Figure 4 numbers are garbled in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fits of held-out loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation from smaller runs to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token allocation trends.
Tests MoE routing/architecture comparisons in antibody language models, not a broad sweep of depth, width, and other architecture choices across language-model families.
No tests of power-law forms in other modalities or in repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes.
Compares downstream classification results for a small set of models, but does not fit a predictive relationship to pretraining loss or establish a general scaling curve.
No analysis of scaling-law fit choices, fitted exponents, or curves bending away from power laws.
